claim: The transition from a unicellular organism to the first multicellular animal occurred more than 600 million years ago.
source: The transition from a unicellular organism to the first multicellular animal, more than 600 million years ago (Budd and Jensen, 2017; dos Reis et al., 2015), marks one of the most radical evolutionary innovations within the eukaryotes.
evidence: Supported by citations to Budd and Jensen, 2017 and dos Reis et al., 2015

claim: The highest levels of organismal complexity, body plan diversity and developmental regulation among eukaryotes are found in the Metazoa.
source: Although multicellularity has independently evolved multiple times in the eukaryotic lineage, the highest levels of organismal complexity, body plan diversity and developmental regulation are found in the Metazoa (Grosberg and Strathmann, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Grosberg and Strathmann, 2007

claim: The animal ancestor was already a genomically complex organism with a rich complement of genes encoding proteins related to a multicellular lifestyle.
source: We now know that the animal ancestor was already a genomically complex organism, with a rich complement of genes encoding proteins related to a multicellular lifestyle.
evidence: Supported by established scientific knowledge from comparative genomics studies

claim: Transcription factors, extracellular matrix components and intricate signaling pathways were present in the animal ancestor before the emergence of multicellularity.
source: These include transcription factors, extracellular matrix components and intricate signaling pathways that were previously considered animal-specific, but were already poised to be co-opted for multicellularity when animals emerged (Fairclough et al., 2013; Suga et al., 2013; Richter and King, 2013; Manning et al., 2008; Suga et al., 2012; de Mendoza et al., 2013; Sebé-Pedrós et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to comparative genomics studies

claim: Metazoa have larger genomes than most other eukaryotes.
source: Furthermore, the genome architectures of extant Metazoa are, in many aspects, markedly different from most other eukaryotes: they have larger genomes (Elliott and Gregory, 2015a)
evidence: Supported by citation to Elliott and Gregory, 2015a

claim: Metazoa have more introns than most other eukaryotes.
source: they have larger genomes (Elliott and Gregory, 2015a), containing more (Csuros et al., 2011) and longer introns (Elliott and Gregory, 2015a)
evidence: Supported by citations to Csuros et al., 2011 and Elliott and Gregory, 2015a

claim: Metazoa have longer introns than most other eukaryotes.
source: containing more (Csuros et al., 2011) and longer introns (Elliott and Gregory, 2015a)
evidence: Supported by citation to Elliott and Gregory, 2015a

claim: Metazoan introns can sustain alternative splicing-rich transcriptomes.
source: containing more (Csuros et al., 2011) and longer introns (Elliott and Gregory, 2015a) that can sustain alternative splicing-rich transcriptomes (McGuire et al., 2008; Irimia and Roy, 2014)
evidence: Supported by citations to McGuire et al., 2008 and Irimia and Roy, 2014

claim: Metazoa have richer complements of repetitive sequences such as transposable elements than most other eukaryotes.
source: have richer complements of repetitive sequences such as transposable elements (Elliott and Gregory, 2015b)
evidence: Supported by citation to Elliott and Gregory, 2015b

claim: Metazoan genomes are structured in ancient patterns of gene linkage associated with transcriptional co-regulation.
source: are structured in ancient patterns of gene linkage associated with transcriptional co-regulation (Irimia et al., 2012; Simakov et al., 2013) – e.g., the Homeobox clusters (Ferrier, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Irimia et al., 2012, Simakov et al., 2013, and Ferrier, 2016

claim: Four new genomes were sequenced for this study: Corallochytrium limacisporum and three Ichthyosporea (Chromosphaera perkinsii, Pirum gemmata, and Abeoforma whisleri).
source: Here, we present the complete genomes of four newly sequenced organisms: Corallochytrium limacisporum and the ichthyosporeans Chromosphaera perkinsii (gen. nov., sp. nov.), Pirum gemmata and Abeoforma whisleri.
evidence: Directly stated in the manuscript as new data generated for this study

claim: The Corallochytrium genome is 24.1 Mb in size.
source: Of the four genomes presented here, Corallochytrium (24.1 Mb) and Chromosphaera (34.6 Mb) have the highest completeness and contiguity (Figure 1).
evidence: Reported as data from genome assembly

claim: The Chromosphaera genome is 34.6 Mb in size.
source: Of the four genomes presented here, Corallochytrium (24.1 Mb) and Chromosphaera (34.6 Mb) have the highest completeness and contiguity (Figure 1).
evidence: Reported as data from genome assembly

claim: Corallochytrium has 7,535 annotated genes.
source: Specifically, Corallochytrium has 7535 genes and 83.4% of the BUSCO paneukaryotic gene set (a proxy to genome completeness (Simão et al., 2015))
evidence: Reported as data from genome annotation

claim: Chromosphaera has 12,463 annotated genes.
source: Chromosphaera has 12,463 annotated genes comprising 85.5% of the BUSCO set
evidence: Reported as data from genome annotation

claim: Chromosphaera perkinsii is a member of Ichthyosporea in the order Dermocystida.
source: We classified the newly identified Chromosphaera perkinsii (gen. nov., sp. nov.) as a member of Ichthyosporea, in the order Dermocystida, as it clusters with Sphaerothecum destruens in our phylogenomic analysis (Figure 2; BS = 100%, BPP = 1).
evidence: Based on phylogenomic analysis data presented in the study

claim: Chromosphaera is the first described putatively free-living dermocystid Ichthyosporea.
source: Therefore, Chromosphaera, isolated from shallow marine sediments in Hawai'i, is the first described putatively free-living dermocystid Ichthyosporea.
evidence: Inferred from phylogenetic classification and isolation source

claim: All described dermocystids are strict vertebrate parasites.
source: Indeed, all described dermocystids are strict vertebrate parasites, whereas ichthyophonids are typical animal commensals or parasites (although free-living species have been described and some have been identified in environmental surveys of marine microbial eukaryotic diversity) (del Campo and Ruiz-Trillo, 2013; Glockling et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to del Campo and Ruiz-Trillo, 2013 and Glockling et al., 2013

claim: Teretosporea, comprising Ichthyosporea and Corallochytrium, are a sister-group to all other holozoans.
source: Our analysis confirms our previous results with regards to the phylogenetic relationships within Holozoa: the Teretosporea, comprising Ichthyosporea and the small free-living osmotroph Corallochytrium (Raghukumar, 1987), are a sister-group to all the other holozoans (filastereans, choanoflagellates and animals) with improved statistical support (Figure 2; BS = 93%, BPP = 0.85).
evidence: Based on phylogenomic analysis data presented in the study

claim: Early-branching animals have genomes in the 300-500 Mb range.
source: We found that Metazoa typically have larger genomes than their unicellular relatives: early-branching animals are within the 300–500 Mb range (Elliott and Gregory, 2015a; Simakov and Kawashima, 2017)
evidence: Supported by citations to Elliott and Gregory, 2015a and Simakov and Kawashima, 2017

claim: Most unicellular holozoans have relatively compact genomes.
source: most unicellular holozoans have relatively compact genomes, like Corallochytrium, Capsaspora or Chromosphaera (24.1, 27.9 and 34.6 Mb, respectively; Figure 3A).
evidence: Based on genome assembly data presented in the study

claim: Sphaeroforma, Abeoforma, Pirum and Ichthyophonus have genomes in the 84.4-120.9 Mb range.
source: There are, however, a few exceptions in the Ichthyosporea: Sphaeroforma, Abeoforma, Pirum and Ichthyophonus have genomes in the 84.4–120.9 Mb range (using assembly length as a proxy to genome size)
evidence: Based on genome assembly data

claim: A parsimonious scenario for genome size evolution implies a holozoan ancestor with a compact genome (24.1-34.6 Mb).
source: A parsimonious scenario for genome size evolution would imply an holozoan ancestor with a fairly compact genome, in line with the values of Corallochytrium, Capsaspora and Chromosphaera (24.1–34.6 Mb)
evidence: Inferred from comparative analysis of genome sizes across holozoans

claim: There were secondary genome expansions in ichthyosporeans.
source: followed by secondary genome expansions in ichthyosporeans (the stem lineage of ichthyophonids, and then again in individual species) and possibly Salpingoeca (55.4 Mb).
evidence: Inferred from comparative analysis of genome sizes

claim: There was another genome expansion at the origin of multicellularity.
source: The largest unicellular holozoan assembled genomes fall short of the inferred C-values of ancestral Metazoa (~300 Mb) (Simakov and Kawashima, 2017), thus indicating another genome expansion at the origin of multicellularity.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of unicellular holozoan genome sizes with ancestral Metazoa estimates

claim: 5-9% of the genome of Salpingoeca, Sphaeroforma, Abeoforma and Pirum are covered by transposable elements.
source: Indeed, 5–9% of the genome of Salpingoeca, Sphaeroforma, Abeoforma and Pirum are covered by TEs, whereas other holozoans are below 2.5% (Figure 3A).
evidence: Based on transposable element annotation data

claim: Other holozoans have less than 2.5% of their genomes covered by transposable elements.
source: Indeed, 5–9% of the genome of Salpingoeca, Sphaeroforma, Abeoforma and Pirum are covered by TEs, whereas other holozoans are below 2.5% (Figure 3A).
evidence: Based on transposable element annotation data

claim: Unicellular holozoans have diverse TE complements, ranging between 42 families in Corallochytrium to >400 in Pirum or Abeoforma.
source: Unicellular holozoan have diverse TE complements, ranging between 42 families in Corallochytrium to >400 in Pirum or Abeoforma (Figure 3—figure supplement 1; [Carr and Suga, 2014])
evidence: Based on transposable element annotation data

claim: Approximately 31% of TE families in unicellular holozoans are shared with metazoan genomes.
source: and ~31% of these families are shared with metazoan genomes (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Based on comparative analysis of TE families

claim: In Salpingoeca, Pirum and Abeoforma, species-specific small sets of TE families with high sequence identity accounted for the vast majority of copies, signaling recent TE invasions.
source: In Salpingoeca, Pirum and Abeoforma, we found species-specific small sets of TE families, sharing high sequence identity, that accounted for the vast majority of copies (Figure 3B). This signaled recent TE invasions, and, therefore, independent contributions to genome expansion.
evidence: Based on analysis of TE sequence similarity and abundance

claim: There were hints of older TE propagation events in Sphaeroforma and Pirum, with a long tail of low-similarity TE copies.
source: There were hints of older TE propagation events in Sphaeroforma and Pirum, with a long tail of low-similarity TE copies (Figure 3B).
evidence: Based on analysis of TE sequence similarity distributions

claim: In Abeoforma and Pirum, TEs and other simple repeats comprised up to 17% and 34% of the genome, respectively.
source: In Abeoforma and Pirum, TEs and other simple repeats comprised up to 17% and 34% of the genome
evidence: Based on repetitive element annotation data

claim: Abeoforma and Pirum have unusually AT-biased nucleotide compositions.
source: accompanied by unusually AT-biased nucleotide compositions (Figure 1A).
evidence: Based on genome composition analysis

claim: The smaller genomes of Corallochytrium and Chromosphaera were largely depleted of repetitive/satellite regions and TEs (1.8% and 3.8% of their genomes).
source: Finally, the smaller genomes of Corallochytrium and Chromosphaera were largely depleted of repetitive/satellite regions and TEs (1.8% and 3.8% of their genomes).
evidence: Based on repetitive element annotation data

claim: Corallochytrium and Chromosphaera underwent a secondary streamlining process.
source: This finding, together with their reduced intron content (see below, Figure 4) suggests a secondary streamlining process.
evidence: Inferred from low TE content and reduced intron content

claim: Microsynteny conservation is common in Metazoa, frequently due to coordinated cis-regulation.
source: Ancestral conservation of gene linkage at the local level (microsynteny) is common in Metazoa, frequently due to coordinated cis-regulation (Irimia et al., 2012; Simakov et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Irimia et al., 2012 and Simakov et al., 2013

claim: Salpingoeca and Monosiga show microsynteny conservation.
source: This hypothesis held true for the Salpingoeca-Monosiga genome pair, but we found little or no conservation in almost all inter-specific comparisons of ichthyosporeans and Corallochytrium.
evidence: Based on microsynteny analysis data

claim: There is little or no microsynteny conservation in almost all inter-specific comparisons of ichthyosporeans and Corallochytrium.
source: This hypothesis held true for the Salpingoeca-Monosiga genome pair, but we found little or no conservation in almost all inter-specific comparisons of ichthyosporeans and Corallochytrium.
evidence: Based on microsynteny analysis data

claim: Creolimax and Sphaeroforma share 907 syntenic orthologous genes.
source: There were, however, two exceptions: Creolimax-Sphaeroforma (sibling species; 907 syntenic orthologous genes) and, to a lesser extent, Chromosphaera-Corallochytrium (72 genes).
evidence: Based on microsynteny analysis data

claim: Chromosphaera and Corallochytrium share 72 syntenic orthologous genes.
source: There were, however, two exceptions: Creolimax-Sphaeroforma (sibling species; 907 syntenic orthologous genes) and, to a lesser extent, Chromosphaera-Corallochytrium (72 genes).
evidence: Based on microsynteny analysis data

claim: Capsaspora shows remarkable across-lineage microsynteny conservation with the distant teretosporeans Chromosphaera (142 genes) and Corallochytrium (129 genes).
source: In contrast, the analysis of microsynteny in Capsaspora revealed remarkable across-lineage conservation with the distant teretosporeans Chromosphaera and Corallochytrium (142 and 129 genes, respectively).
evidence: Based on microsynteny analysis data

claim: Capsaspora retains a few shared linked gene pairs with Trichoplax, cnidarians Aiptasia sp. and Nematostella vectensis, and sponges Amphimedon queenslandica and Oscarella carmela.
source: Moreover, and to a lesser degree, Capsaspora also retains a few shared linked gene pairs with Trichoplax, the cnidarians Aiptasia sp., Nematostella vectensis, and the sponges Amphimedon queenslandica and Oscarella carmela (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Based on microsynteny analysis data

claim: Integrin-α and integrin-β genes from Corallochytrium (one pair) and Capsaspora (four pairs) are in a conserved head-to-head arrangement of likely holozoan origin.
source: Indeed, integrin-α and integrin-β genes from Corallochytrium (one pair) and Capsaspora (four pairs) are in a conserved head-to-head arrangement of likely holozoan origin.
evidence: Based on gene arrangement analysis

claim: Capsaspora's pairs of collinear α/β integrins co-express during its life cycle.
source: Incidentally, Capsaspora's pairs of collinear α/β integrins co-express during its life cycle (Sebé-Pedrós et al., 2013)
evidence: Supported by citation to Sebé-Pedrós et al., 2013

claim: Capsaspora, Chromosphaera and Ichthyophonus accumulated fewer amino-acidic substitutions per alignment position than choanoflagellates since their divergence from animals.
source: In all comparisons, Capsaspora, Chromosphaera and Ichthyophonus accumulated fewer amino-acidic substitutions per alignment position than choanoflagellates since their divergence from animals (p<0.05 in Wilcoxon rank sum test).
evidence: Based on phylogenetic distance analysis with statistical testing

claim: Corallochytrium was singled out as the taxon with more cumulative amino acid differences with animals.
source: Conversely, Corallochytrium was singled out as the taxon with more cumulative amino acid differences with animals.
evidence: Based on phylogenetic distance analysis

claim: The last common ancestor of Metazoa is inferred to have had the highest intron density among eukaryotes.
source: Indeed, the last common ancestor (LCA) of Metazoa is inferred to have had the highest intron density among eukaryotes, due to a process of continuous intron gain starting in the last eukaryotic common ancestor (LECA) (Csuros et al., 2011; Carmel et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Csuros et al., 2011 and Carmel et al., 2007

claim: High intron density provides physical space for transcription regulatory sites.
source: provides physical space for transcription regulatory sites (Le Hir et al., 2003; Sebé-Pedrós et al., 2016b)
evidence: Supported by citations to Le Hir et al., 2003 and Sebé-Pedrós et al., 2016b

claim: High intron density facilitates the diversification of gene families by exon shuffling.
source: and facilitates the diversification of gene families by exon shuffling (Liu et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Liu et al., 2005

claim: Many ichthyosporeans, choanoflagellates and animals have a high number of introns per gene.
source: Our survey of intron richness across eukaryotes identifies a high number of introns per gene in many ichthyosporeans, choanoflagellates and animals (Figure 4A).
evidence: Based on intron content analysis data

claim: Creolimax and Ichthyophonus harbor longer introns than most protistan eukaryotes, similar in length to those of some animals.
source: Moreover, Creolimax and Ichthyophonus harbor longer introns than most protistan eukaryotes, similar in length to those of some animals (Figure 4B).
evidence: Based on intron length analysis data

claim: There were two independent periods of intense intron gain in unicellular holozoans: at LCA of Metazoa and Choanoflagellata, and in the branch leading to ichthyophonid Ichthyosporea.
source: This analysis supports the second hypothesis and reveals two independent periods of intense intron gain in unicellular holozoans: at LCA of Metazoa and Choanoflagellata, and in the branch leading to ichthyophonid Ichthyosporea (Figure 5A–B).
evidence: Based on ancestral reconstruction of intron evolution

claim: After animals and choanoflagellates diverged, intron gains independently persisted in both lineages.
source: After animals and choanoflagellates diverged, intron gains independently persisted in both lineages.
evidence: Based on ancestral reconstruction of intron evolution

claim: A prolonged process of intron gain can be observed in the lines of descent from the LECA (4.9-5.5 introns per kbp of coding sequence) to Ichthyophonida (6.9 introns/CDS kbp) and Metazoa LCAs (8.7 introns/CDS kbp).
source: A prolonged process of intron gain can be observed, however, in the lines of descent from the LECA (4.9–5.5 introns per kbp of coding sequence) to Ichthyophonida (6.9 introns/CDS kbp) and Metazoa LCAs (8.7 introns/CDS kbp)
evidence: Based on ancestral reconstruction of intron evolution

claim: The intron-rich Creolimax and Sphaeroforma form an independent cluster that differs from the Holozoa LCA in their pattern of shared introns.
source: Second, ichthyosporeans and Corallochytrium, although phylogenetically closely-related to each other, are highly divergent in their pattern of shared introns: the intron-dense Creolimax and Sphaeroforma form an independent cluster that differs from the Holozoa LCA
evidence: Based on hierarchical clustering analysis of intron presence/absence

claim: Corallochytrium and Chromosphaera underwent independent secondary simplifications in intron content.
source: whereas Corallochytrium and Chromosphaera undergo independent secondary simplifications (from 5.5 introns/CDS kbp in the Teretosporea LCA, to 0.0 and 0.7, respectively).
evidence: Based on ancestral reconstruction and comparison of intron densities

claim: 85.5% of Capsaspora's introns are of holozoan or earlier origin.
source: In contrast, Capsaspora (3.5 intron/CDS kbp) appears to have undergone little ancestral reconfiguration of its gene architecture: there is an equilibrium between few losses and gains at the root of Filozoa (Figure 5A), and 85.5% of its introns are of holozoan or earlier origin (Figure 6B).
evidence: Based on phylostratigraphic analysis of intron origins

claim: Introns with regulatory sites from Capsaspora have a similar, ancestral-biased, age distribution as all introns.
source: Interestingly, introns with regulatory sites from Capsaspora (identified in [Sebé-Pedrós et al., 2016b]) have a similar, ancestral-biased, age distribution (Fisher's exact test, p-value=1; Figure 6B).
evidence: Based on phylostratigraphic analysis with statistical testing

claim: There is a decoupling between the evolutionary dynamics of introns and regulatory sites in Capsaspora, despite sharing physical space in the genome.
source: This hints at a decoupling between the evolutionary dynamics of introns and regulatory sites, despite sharing physical space in the genome.
evidence: Inferred from similar age distributions of introns with and without regulatory sites

claim: The core NMD toolkit has a pan-eukaryotic distribution.
source: The core NMD toolkit (consisting of the Upf1-3, Smg1, Smg5/6/7 and Smg8/9 genes; the release factors 1 and 3; and the exon-junction complex [EJC] [He and Jacobson, 2015]) has a pan-eukaryotic distribution (Figure 5C-Figure 5—figure supplement 2A), as previously reported for the wider spliceosomal molecular machinery (Collins and Penny, 2005).
evidence: Based on ortholog identification across eukaryotes and supported by citation to Collins and Penny, 2005

claim: The NMD toolkit was fully conserved in the LCAs of Ichthyophonida, Metazoa and Metazoa + Choanoflagellata.
source: The NMD toolkit was also fully conserved in the LCAs of Ichthyophonida, Metazoa and Metazoa + Choanoflagellata – which underwent the above-reported intron gain episodes (Figure 5A).
evidence: Based on ancestral reconstruction of gene presence

claim: The SR splicing factors appeared early in eukaryotic evolution and were conserved in LCAs ranging from Opisthokonta to Metazoa.
source: Similarly, the SR splicing factors (serine/arginine-rich proteins, termed SRSF1-9 and TRA2A/B in humans), which are involved in splice site recognition in metazoan AS (Plass et al., 2008; Sanford et al., 2005), also appeared early in eukaryotic evolution and were conserved in LCAs ranging from Opisthokonta to Metazoa (Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Based on ancestral reconstruction of gene presence and supported by citations

claim: Corallochytrium secondarily lost part of its NMD machinery and SR splicing factors concomitantly with its acute intron losses.
source: Interestingly, Corallochytrium secondarily lost part of its NMD machinery and SR splicing factors (e.g., it lacks three out of four EJC components, and only possesses one canonical SR gene) concomitantly with its acute intron losses
evidence: Based on ortholog identification and intron content analysis

claim: The intron gain episodes of the LCAs of ichthyophonids and animals occurred in ancestral holozoans that were potentially able to perform NMD of aberrant transcripts.
source: Thus, we found that the intron gain episodes of the LCAs of ichthyophonids and animals occurred in ancestral holozoans that were potentially able to perform NMD of aberrant transcripts.
evidence: Inferred from conservation of NMD machinery in relevant ancestors

claim: Protein domain rearrangements, combined with gene duplication, allow for functional diversification of gene families.
source: This mechanism, combined with gene duplication, allows for a functional diversification of gene families by tuning the interactions with other components of the cell—its substrate specificities, sub-cellular localization or partnerships with other proteins within larger complexes.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of protein evolution

claim: Protein domain rearrangements are credited with the diversification of many gene families involved in complex signaling and/or multicellular integrated lifestyle in Metazoa.
source: Albeit protein domain rearrangements are not uncommon in eukaryotes (Basu et al., 2008, Basu et al., 2009; Leonard and Richards, 2012), this process is specifically credited with the diversification of many gene families involved in complex signaling and/or multicellular integrated lifestyle in Metazoa (Suga et al., 2012; Simakov and Kawashima, 2017; Sebé-Pedrós et al., 2010; Tordai et al., 2005; Ekman et al., 2007; Hynes, 2012; Deshmukh et al., 2010; Grau-Bové et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: There was a consistent pattern of creation of protein domain architectures in the lineage leading to Metazoa, specifically from the opisthokont to the bilaterian LCA.
source: In this scenario of pervasive domain rearrangements, we identified a consistent pattern of creation of protein domain architectures in the lineage leading to Metazoa – specifically, the line of descent from the opisthokont to the bilaterian LCA (Figure 7A–B).
evidence: Based on ancestral reconstruction of protein domain combinations

claim: The tendency for creation of protein domain architectures was most acute at three points in animal prehistory: the Holozoa LCA, the Filozoa LCA, and the Metazoa LCA.
source: This tendency was most acute at three points in animal prehistory: the Holozoa LCA, the Filozoa LCA (Capsaspora, animals and choanoflagellates) and the Metazoa LCA.
evidence: Based on ancestral reconstruction of protein domain combinations

claim: The increased diversity of protein organizations in animals has its roots in successive events of domain shuffling during their unicellular holozoan prehistory.
source: Our analysis thus shows that the increased diversity of protein organizations in animals has its roots in successive events of domain shuffling during their unicellular holozoan prehistory, even if this period was dominated by a relative stasis in terms of the emergence of new protein domain families (Figure 7A and Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Based on ancestral reconstruction of protein domain combinations and individual domains

claim: Gene families carrying TF- and ECM-related domains had consistently higher diversification rates not only in Metazoa but also in their unicellular ancestors.
source: We found that gene families carrying TF- and ECM-related domains had consistently higher diversification rates not only in Metazoa but also in their unicellular ancestors (Figure 7B, right panel; asterisks indicate two-fold differences).
evidence: Based on analysis of domain combination gain/loss ratios for functional subsets

claim: There is a continuous process of protein diversity gain involving multicellularity-related genes in animal ancestors ranging from the LCA of Obazoa to the LCA of Metazoa.
source: We thus identify a continuous process of protein diversity gain involving multicellularity-related genes in animal ancestors ranging from the LCA of Obazoa (Opisthokonta + Apusomonadida) to the LCA of Metazoa.
evidence: Inferred from higher diversification rates of TF and ECM genes across ancestors

claim: At the genome level, gene family diversification tends to reduce modularity due to the use of highly promiscuous protein domains.
source: Second, there was a strong negative relationship between modularity and the number of protein domains per gene family (Spearman's rank correlation coefficient, ρs=−0.96, p<0.001, Figure 8B). Therefore, at the genome level, gene family diversification tends to reduce modularity due to the use of highly promiscuous protein domains, as it has been frequently reported in animals (Simakov and Kawashima, 2017; Basu et al., 2008).
evidence: Based on network modularity analysis with statistical testing and supported by citations

claim: The diversification of gene families with domains related to the ECM, signaling, ubiquitination or protein-protein interactions occurs by acquisition of promiscuous domains that reduce their modularity.
source: This same effect was observed when we analyzed subsets of the proteome networks sharing a common function: the diversification of gene families with domains related to the ECM, signaling, ubiquitination or protein–protein interactions occurs by acquisition of promiscuous domains that reduce their modularity (with ρs in the range −0.32 to −0.84 and p<0.001; Figure 8—figure supplement 1A–D)
evidence: Based on network modularity analysis of functional subsets with statistical testing

claim: Animal TF genes have more exclusive domains than their unicellular ancestors or relatives.
source: However, the analysis of the transcription factor domain sub-networks exhibited an opposite signal: animal TF genes have more exclusive domains than their unicellular ancestors or relatives (reflected by higher modularities; Figure 8A, lower panel).
evidence: Based on network modularity analysis of TF subnetwork

claim: There was no negative relationship between the number of domains per community and the network modularity for transcription factors.
source: Also, there was no negative relationship between the number of domains per community and the network modularity (ρs=0.12, p-value=0.32), meaning that the addition of new domains to TF genes occurred in a gene family-specific manner (Figure 8B).
evidence: Based on network modularity analysis with statistical testing

claim: The expanded TF repertoires of animal genomes preferentially diversify their protein domain architectures by acquiring new, not promiscuous, domains.
source: This implies that the expanded TF repertoires of animal genomes (de Mendoza et al., 2013) preferentially diversify their protein domain architectures by acquiring new, not promiscuous, domains.
evidence: Inferred from lack of negative relationship between modularity and domains per community in TF subnetwork

claim: There is a distinct dynamics of protein domain rearrangements for TF families in the LCA of Metazoa: new domains tend to be acquired in a family-specific manner.
source: In summary, we identify a distinct dynamics of protein domain rearrangements for TF families in the LCA of Metazoa: new domains tend to be acquired in a family-specific manner (as opposed to reuse of promiscuous domains), contributing to the functional specialization of the animal TF repertoire.
evidence: Inferred from network modularity analysis of TF subnetwork

claim: LIM-associated homeobox genes were identified in multiple ichthyosporeans, Corallochytrium and Capsaspora.
source: However, we identified LIM-associated homeobox genes in multiple ichthyosporeans, Corallochytrium and Capsaspora.
evidence: Based on homolog identification and phylogenetic analysis

claim: Bona fide LIM-HD homologs with 1-2 LIM domains were identified in Corallochytrium, Chromosphaera, Ichthyophonus, Amoebidium and Capsaspora.
source: Our analysis identified bona fide LIM-HD homologs with 1–2 LIM domains in Corallochytrium, Chromosphaera, Ichthyophonus, Amoebidium and Capsaspora (which had 1–2 LIM domains and a homeodomain)
evidence: Based on phylogenetic analysis and domain architecture analysis

claim: None of the unicellular holozoan LIM-HD genes could be confidently assigned to animal LIM homeodomain subfamilies.
source: None of the unicellular holozoan LIM-HD genes could be confidently assigned to animal LIM homeodomain subfamilies (Lhx1/5, Lhx3/4, Lmx, Islet, Lhx2/9, Lhx6/8), probably because they emerged before LIM-HD radiation in animals.
evidence: Based on phylogenetic analysis

claim: The KIX-Bromodomain-DUF902 protein domain architecture of p300/CBP was identified in both Capsaspora and ichthyosporeans.
source: We identified this protein domain architecture in both Capsaspora and ichthyosporeans, which also have the CREB gene (Sebé-Pedrós et al., 2011).
evidence: Based on domain architecture analysis and supported by citation

claim: Capsaspora's epigenome contains p300/CBP-specific histone acetylation marks, but its relatively compact genome lacks distal enhancers.
source: Intriguingly, Capsaspora's epigenome contains p300/CBP-specific histone acetylation marks, but its relatively compact genome lacks distal enhancers (Sebé-Pedrós et al., 2016b).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sebé-Pedrós et al., 2016b

claim: A canonical type IV collagen gene was found in the filasterean Ministeria vibrans.
source: We found, however, a remarkable exception: a canonical type IV collagen gene in the filasterean Ministeria vibrans, a naked filose amoeba devoid of basement membrane or ECM (Patterson et al., 1993; Cavalier-Smith and Chao, 2003).
evidence: Based on homolog identification and phylogenetic analysis, with citations for Ministeria characteristics

claim: The Ministeria type IV collagen ortholog is composed of a pair of C4 domains at the C-terminus and multiple collagen Gly-X-Y repeats.
source: This Ministeria ortholog is composed of a pair of C4 domains at the C-terminus and multiple collagen Gly-X-Y repeats.
evidence: Based on domain architecture analysis

claim: The C4 domain arrangement in type IV collagen appeared from two duplicated motifs within the same protein, and its order is thoroughly conserved in animals and Ministeria.
source: Phylogenetic analysis of C4 showed that this domain arrangement appeared from two duplicated motifs within the same protein, and its order is thoroughly conserved in animals and Ministeria (Figure 9E).
evidence: Based on phylogenetic analysis

claim: A canonical type IV collagen was already present in the common ancestor of filastereans, choanoflagellates and animals.
source: Thus, a canonical type IV collagen was already present in the common ancestor of filastereans, choanoflagellates and animals – which was unicellular and most likely lacked ECM or basement membrane-like structures.
evidence: Inferred from presence in Ministeria and phylogenetic analysis

claim: The essential role of collagen IV in the organization of extant metazoans' tissues would require a co-option from an earlier function in a unicellular context.
source: The essential role of collagen IV in the organization of extant metazoans' tissues (Fidler et al., 2017) would therefore require a co-option from an earlier function in a unicellular context, as it has been previously proposed for other ECM components such as the integrin adhesome (Sebé-Pedrós et al., 2010) or cadherins (Abedin and King, 2008).
evidence: Inferred from presence in unicellular ancestor and supported by citations for similar cases

claim: There was a continued process of gene innovation in terms of protein domain architectures in the animal ancestry, peaking at the LCA of Holozoa.
source: We have identified continued process of gene innovation in terms of protein domain architectures in the animal ancestry, peaking at the LCA of Holozoa.
evidence: Based on ancestral reconstruction of protein domain combinations

claim: The burst of diversification at the LCA of Holozoa was enriched in TFs and ECM-related domains.
source: This burst of diversification, enriched in TFs and ECM-related domains (Figure 7B), set the foundations of the animal-like gene tool-kits of unicellular holozoans
evidence: Based on analysis of domain combination gain/loss ratios for functional subsets

claim: Three independent episodes of massive intron gain were detected: at the root of Metazoa, the shared LCA between Metazoa and Choanoflagellata, and the root of ichthyophonid Ichthyosporea.
source: We detect three independent episodes of massive intron gain: (1) at the root of Metazoa, (2) the shared LCA between Metazoa and Choanoflagellata, and (3) the root of ichthyophonid Ichthyosporea (Creolimax, Sphaeroforma and Ichthyophonus).
evidence: Based on ancestral reconstruction of intron evolution

claim: Since the early origin of introns in the earliest eukaryotes, the ancestry of both animals and ichthyophonids maintained a state of high intron density.
source: Furthermore, since the early origin of introns in the earliest eukaryotes (Irimia and Roy, 2014), the ancestry of both animals and ichthyophonids maintained a state of high intron density.
evidence: Based on ancestral reconstruction of intron evolution and supported by citation

claim: Animal transcriptomes are rich in isoform-producing exon skipping.
source: First, the independent intron gain episodes of animals and unicellular holozoans are mirrored by two different modes of alternative splicing dominating in each clade: animal transcriptomes are rich in isoform-producing exon skipping (McGuire et al., 2008; Irimia and Roy, 2014)
evidence: Supported by citations to McGuire et al., 2008 and Irimia and Roy, 2014

claim: Most of the alternatively spliced transcripts of Capsaspora and Creolimax originate by intron retention.
source: whereas most of the alternatively spliced transcripts of Capsaspora (Sebé-Pedrós et al., 2013) and Creolimax (de Mendoza et al., 2015) originate by intron retention
evidence: Supported by citations to Sebé-Pedrós et al., 2013 and de Mendoza et al., 2015

claim: Capsaspora emerges as a well-suited model with a slow pace of genomic change attested for multiple traits: intron evolution, coding sequence conservation, gene order and possibly genome size.
source: Interestingly, Capsaspora emerges as a well-suited model with a slow pace of genomic change attested for multiple traits: intron evolution, coding sequence conservation, gene order and (possibly) genome size.
evidence: Inferred from multiple analyses of genomic traits

claim: Capsaspora's remarkable microsynteny conservation with Corallochytrium and Chromosphaera indicates the existence of ancestral holozoan gene linkages that have been disrupted and rewired in extant choanoflagellates, ichthyosporeans and animals.
source: Its remarkable microsynteny conservation with Corallochytrium and Chromosphaera indicates the existence of ancestral holozoan gene linkages that have been disrupted, and rewired, in extant choanoflagellates, ichthyosporeans and animals (Figure 3C).
evidence: Inferred from microsynteny conservation patterns

claim: Holozoan genomes evolved under temporally uncoupled dynamics for synteny reorganization, intron gains, TE propagation, coding sequence conservation and gene family diversification.
source: In particular, we have observed that holozoan genomes evolved under temporally uncoupled dynamics for synteny reorganization, intron gains, TE propagation, coding sequence conservation and gene family diversification.
evidence: Inferred from multiple independent analyses of different genomic traits

claim: The diversification of ECM and TF gene families extends back to the LCA of Holozoa.
source: Yet, other traits exhibit conserved dynamics across the unicellularity/multicellularity divide: the diversification of ECM and TF gene families—including molecular tool-kits essential for multicellularity—extends back to the LCA of Holozoa
evidence: Based on ancestral reconstruction of protein domain combinations

claim: The high intron densities in premetazoans suggest a continued state of transcriptome variability, co-optable for regulation or protein innovation, in the unicellular prehistory of Metazoa.
source: and the high intron densities in premetazoans suggest a continued state of transcriptome variability, co-optable for regulation or protein innovation, in the unicellular prehistory of Metazoa.
evidence: Inferred from intron density patterns in premetazoan ancestors
